Technical article · HTML series, part 4

Images, Audio, and Video

The img, picture and source elements, srcset, sizes and alt; image formats from JPEG to AVIF; dimensions, lazy loading and optimisation; audio, video and track with controls, autoplay, muting, looping, posters and captions; and the other ways to embed content: iframe, embed, object, canvas and svg, with the cross-origin rules that govern them. Grounded in the HTML Living Standard, the format specifications, MDN and WCAG.

Updated 14 November 2026125 references (Vancouver style)Includes real sample media, exercises, trivia, a srcset simulator and a live playground

The first article in this series covered how an HTML document is built, the second the text inside it, and the third the links between documents. This one is about everything that is not text. The first list of HTML tags had no way to show a picture;1 on 25 February 1993 Marc Andreessen, who was working on the Mosaic browser, proposed a new empty tag, IMG, with a single required SRC attribute naming the image file.2 Three decades later the img element is joined by picture, audio, video, iframe, canvas and inline svg, all of which the HTML standard calls embedded content.3,4

Every image, sound and video clip in this article is real and embedded in this one file, so the examples play and render without a network connection. Section 2 covers images, section 3 audio and video, and section 4 the other embedded content. Sections 6 to 10 hold exercises, trivia questions, a srcset simulator, a playground and a quick-reference table.

1Introduction

1.1 Where embedded content is defined

The HTML Living Standard5 defines the elements in its §4.8 Embedded content and, for canvas, in §4.12 Scripting.3,6 The file formats themselves are defined elsewhere, by ITU, W3C, IETF and the Alliance for Open Media, and accessibility requirements come from WCAG.7–11

Table 1. Where the features in this article are specified
SourceWhat it defines
HTML §4.8.1 to §4.8.412–15picture, source, img, srcset, sizes, image selection and the rules for alt text
HTML §4.8.5 to §4.8.716–18iframe, embed and object
HTML §4.8.8 to §4.8.1119–22video, audio, track and the shared media element API
HTML §4.8.16, §4.8.17, §4.12.56,23,24SVG in HTML, width and height, and canvas
HTML §2.5.4, §2.5.7, §2.5.925–27crossorigin, loading and fetchpriority
Format specifications7–10,28,29JPEG, PNG, GIF, SVG, WebP and AVIF
W3C WebVTT30The caption and subtitle file format used by track
WCAG 2.211Text alternatives, captions, audio description and control of moving media

1.2 What makes content "embedded"

The standard defines embedded content as content that imports another resource into the document, or content from another vocabulary (MathML or SVG) that is inserted into the document. Its list is audio, canvas, embed, iframe, img, math, object, picture, svg and video.4 Most of these are replaced elements: the browser does not render their children as ordinary content but replaces the element's box with something else, such as a decoded image, a video frame or a whole nested document.31 That is why an img has no closing tag and why the text inside a video element is shown only by browsers that cannot play video at all.14,19

1.3 A very short history

HTML later gained object, a general element for external resources of any type, but in practice the web settled on specific elements for specific media.18,32 For about fifteen years, audio and video needed a browser plugin, most often Adobe Flash Player; HTML5 added native audio and video elements with a scripting API, and Adobe stopped supporting Flash Player on 31 December 2020.22,33 The applet element, once used to embed Java programs, is now listed among the standard's obsolete features,34 and the standard treats plugins as a legacy concept and describes embed and object mostly in terms of what browsers do without them.17,35

Images have changed just as much. The srcset and sizes attributes and the picture element were added so that one img can choose between several files for different screens.15,36 Native lazy loading followed with the loading attribute, and formats moved from JPEG, PNG and GIF towards WebP and AVIF.26,37

1.4 Media and accessibility

Non-text content is invisible to some users and inaudible to others. WCAG's very first success criterion asks for a text alternative for all non-text content, and its guideline 1.2 asks for captions, transcripts and audio description for time-based media.11,38 The table below lists the criteria that matter most for this article.

Table 2. WCAG 2.2 success criteria that apply to images and media
CriterionLevelIn short
1.1.1 Non-text Content38AImages, controls and other non-text content have a text alternative; decorative ones are hidden from assistive technology
1.2.1 Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded)39AA transcript for audio-only content; a transcript or audio track for silent video
1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded)40ACaptions for all prerecorded audio in synchronised media
1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative41AAudio description or a full text alternative for prerecorded video
1.2.4 Captions (Live)42AACaptions for live audio in synchronised media
1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded)43AAAudio description for prerecorded video
1.4.2 Audio Control44AAudio that plays automatically for more than 3 seconds can be paused, stopped or turned down
1.4.5 Images of Text45AAUse real text rather than pictures of text, except for logos and essential cases
2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide46AMoving content that starts automatically and lasts more than 5 seconds can be paused
2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold47ANothing flashes more than three times in any one second
Captions or subtitles?In WCAG and in HTML, captions are for viewers who cannot hear the audio: they include speaker names and important sounds as well as dialogue. Subtitles translate the dialogue for viewers who can hear but do not understand the language.21,48

2Images

2.1 The img element

FlowPhrasingEmbeddedPalpableVoid (no end tag)Role: img / none

An img element represents an image. It is a void element, so it has no content and no end tag, and its src attribute must be present and contain the URL of a non-interactive, optionally animated image that is neither paged nor scripted.14 An SVG file loaded through img is therefore shown as a picture only: its scripts do not run, its links cannot be followed and it cannot load other external files.14,49

Table 3. Attributes of the img element
AttributeValuePurpose
srcURLThe image (required); also the fallback when srcset is not supported
altText, or emptyThe text alternative (§2.2)
srcset, sizesCandidate list; size listResponsive image candidates (§2.3, §2.4)
width, heightIntegers (CSS pixels)Intrinsic dimensions and aspect ratio (§2.8)
loadinglazy | eagerDefer off-screen images (§2.9)
decodingsync | async | autoHint about decoding the image off the main thread
fetchpriorityhigh | low | autoRelative priority of the request
crossoriginanonymous | use-credentialsFetch with CORS, so a canvas can read the pixels (§4.7)
referrerpolicyPolicy tokenWhich referrer to send with the request
usemap, ismap#name; booleanClient-side and server-side image maps

Source: HTML §4.8.3 The img element, §2.5.4, §2.5.7 and §2.5.9.14,25–27

A basic imageHTML
<img src="scene.jpg" alt="A cartoon landscape: green hills under a blue sky with a low yellow sun"
     width="480" height="320" style="max-width:100%;height:auto">
Rendered in your browser

The style in that example is the one rule nearly every site applies to its images: max-width: 100% stops a large image overflowing a narrow screen, and height: auto keeps its aspect ratio when the width shrinks.36 Section 2.8 explains why the width and height attributes should still be there.

2.2 The alt attribute

The alt attribute gives the image's text alternative. The standard's rule of thumb is that the alternative should be what you would write if you were reading the page aloud to someone over the phone, so it depends on the image's purpose in its context, not on what the image looks like.50 An empty value, alt="", says that the image is not a key part of the content (it is decorative, or it repeats nearby text), and browsers and assistive technology may then ignore it entirely.50,51 A missing alt attribute is different: it tells assistive technology nothing, and many screen readers then fall back to reading the file name.52

alt text depends on the image's jobHTML
<p><a href="#alt"><img src="scene.svg" alt="Home" width="90" height="60"></a>
  An image that is the only content of a link: alt names the destination.</p>
<p><img src="scene.jpg" alt="" width="90" height="60">
  Sunset hills. (Decorative here, because the caption already says it: alt="".)</p>
<p><img src="scene.jpg" alt="Sunset over two green hills" width="90" height="60">
  An informative image with nothing else describing it.</p>
Rendered in your browser

An image that is the only content of a link: alt names the destination.

Sunset hills. (Decorative here, because the caption already says it: alt="".)

An informative image with nothing else describing it.

Avoid

Unhelpful alt valuesHTML
<img src="IMG_4022.jpg">
<img src="chart.png" alt="chart">
<img src="logo.svg" alt="image of logo">
<img src="rule.png" alt="decorative line">

Missing alt, a vague one-word label, "image of", and a description of something that should have been silent.52,54

Prefer

Purposeful alt valuesHTML
<img src="IMG_4022.jpg" alt="Our team at the 2026 summit in Lisbon">
<img src="chart.png" alt="Sales rose 40% from 2024 to 2026; details in table 2">
<img src="logo.svg" alt="Example Co.">
<img src="rule.png" alt="">

Describe the meaning, point to a fuller description for complex images, give a logo the organisation's name, and silence decoration.52,55,56

title is not altThe title attribute is a tooltip. It is not shown to touch-screen or keyboard users and is not a reliable substitute for alt; the standard says it should not be used as the only text alternative for an image.50

2.3 srcset: offering candidates

The srcset attribute lists image candidate strings, separated by commas. Each is a URL followed by an optional descriptor: a pixel-density descriptor such as 2x, or a width descriptor such as 640w giving the file's real width in pixels. One srcset must not mix the two kinds, and two candidates must not have the same descriptor.57 The browser then picks one candidate. The standard deliberately leaves the choice to the browser, which may prefer a smaller file on a slow or metered connection, and may keep using a larger image it already has in its cache.15,58

Density descriptors: the same layout size, sharper on high-DPI screensHTML
<img src="cand-1x.svg"
     srcset="cand-1x.svg 1x, cand-2x.svg 2x"
     alt="Demo: the label shows which candidate your browser chose" width="300" height="168">
Rendered in your browser

Density descriptors suit images that always have the same display size, such as a logo or an avatar. On a screen with a device-pixel ratio of 2 (most phones and many laptops) your browser should have chosen the red "2x" file; on a standard screen, the blue "1x" file.36 The rendered size stays 300 × 168 CSS pixels either way, because a 2x image is drawn at half its pixel size.58

Width descriptors: the browser knows each file's widthHTML
<img src="cand-640.svg"
     srcset="cand-320.svg 320w,
             cand-640.svg 640w,
             cand-1280.svg 1280w"
     sizes="(min-width: 1100px) 640px, 90vw"
     alt="Demo: the label shows which width candidate your browser chose"
     width="640" height="360" style="max-width:100%;height:auto">
Rendered in your browser

2.4 sizes: how wide the slot will be

With width descriptors the browser also needs to know how wide the image will be displayed, before any CSS has loaded. The sizes attribute tells it: a comma-separated list of media conditions, each followed by a length, ending in a length with no condition. The browser uses the length of the first condition that matches.57 Lengths may use px, em, vw or calc(), but not percentages. If sizes is missing, the browser assumes 100vw, the full viewport width.36,57

sizes="auto" for lazy imagesFor an image with loading="lazy", the standard now allows sizes="auto" (or a list that starts with auto,). Because a lazy image is only fetched once layout is known, the browser can use the image's real laid-out width instead of a guess.26,57 Browsers without support fall back to the rest of the list, so write sizes="auto, (min-width: 1100px) 640px, 90vw".

2.5 The picture element

FlowPhrasingEmbeddedContent: source*, then one imgNo role of its own

A picture element contains zero or more source elements followed by exactly one img, optionally mixed with script-supporting elements. It does not display anything itself: it gives the img more sources to choose from.12 The img is still the element that is rendered, that has the alt text and that scripts read through currentSrc.12,59 There are two reasons to use it.36,60

  • Art direction: showing a different crop or composition at different viewport sizes, chosen with the media attribute.
  • Format switching: offering modern formats such as AVIF and WebP with a JPEG or PNG fallback, chosen with the type attribute.
Format switching with a JPEG fallbackHTML
<picture>
  <source srcset="scene.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="scene.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="scene.jpg" alt="Green hills under a low yellow sun"
       width="480" height="320" style="max-width:100%;height:auto">
</picture>
Rendered in your browser
Art direction: a tighter crop on narrow screensHTML
<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="scene-crop.jpg" width="280" height="280">
  <img src="scene.jpg" alt="The sun setting behind the hills"
       width="480" height="320" style="max-width:100%;height:auto">
</picture>
Rendered in your browser

Narrow your browser window below 600 pixels and the second example switches to a square crop centred on the sun. The width and height on the source give that crop its own aspect ratio, so the browser can reserve the right space for whichever file it picks.13,24

2.6 The source element in picture

Void (no end tag)Only inside picture, audio or video

The source element has two jobs depending on its parent. Inside picture it takes srcset (required), sizes, media, type, width and height, and it must not have src. Inside audio or video it takes src (required) and type, and must not have srcset, sizes or media-based image attributes (section 3.2).13

Table 4. source attributes inside picture
AttributeUseExample
srcsetCandidates, exactly as on imgsrcset="a-800.avif 800w, a-1600.avif 1600w"
sizesSlot sizes for width descriptorssizes="(min-width: 60em) 50vw, 100vw"
mediaA media query that must matchmedia="(orientation: portrait)"
typeA MIME type that must be supportedtype="image/avif"
width, heightDimensions of this source's imageswidth="800" height="800"

Source: HTML §4.8.2 The source element.13

2.7 Image formats

Browsers detect an image's format from its first bytes, not from its file extension, and support six formats almost universally.37 They fall into two families: raster formats store a grid of pixels, and vector formats store shapes that are drawn at whatever size is needed. Raster formats differ in how they compress the grid: lossless compression reproduces every pixel exactly, while lossy compression throws away detail the eye is unlikely to miss.37

Table 5. The six common web image formats
FormatMIME typeCompressionTransparencyAnimationBest for
JPEG (1992)7image/jpegLossy (DCT)NoNoPhotographs, where AVIF/WebP are not available
PNG8image/pngLosslessFull alphaYes, as APNGScreenshots, diagrams, images needing exact pixels
GIF (1987, 89a)28image/gifLossless, 256-colour paletteOne colour, on or offYesLegacy; replace animations with video
SVG29image/svg+xmlVector (XML text)YesYes (SMIL, CSS)Icons, logos, diagrams
WebP9image/webpLossy or losslessFull alphaYesPhotos and graphics; very wide support
AVIF10image/avifLossy or lossless (AV1)Full alphaYesPhotos; also HDR and wide colour gamut

Sources: the format specifications and MDN's image file type guide.7–10,28,29,37

MDN gives typical savings over JPEG of 25 to 35 per cent for lossy WebP and about 50 per cent for lossy AVIF, and records support for AVIF in Chrome 85, Firefox 93 and Safari 16.1 onwards.37 The comparison below is real: the same 480 × 320 picture was encoded into each format for this article, and every file is embedded in this page.

Animated GIFs are video in disguiseAn animated GIF stores every frame as a separate palette image, so it is usually far larger than the same clip as a muted, looping video in MP4 or WebM, or as an animated WebP or AVIF.37,61 Section 3.6 shows the video replacement.

2.8 Image dimensions

The width and height attributes give the image's dimensions in CSS pixels, as valid non-negative integers; they are not a way to resize a large image, and they must not be used to stretch an image to a different aspect ratio.24 Their most important job today is to reserve space. Browsers map the two attributes to the CSS aspect-ratio property, so even with width: 100%; height: auto in the stylesheet, the browser can compute the box's height before the image file arrives.24,62

Without them, the image's box starts with no height and the text below it jumps down when the file loads. Google's Core Web Vitals measure such jumps as Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS); web.dev advises that a good CLS score is 0.1 or less and names images without dimensions as a common cause of poor scores.63,64

Dimensions plus object-fit: fitting an image into a fixed boxHTML
<div style="display:flex;gap:12px;flex-wrap:wrap;font:13px system-ui,sans-serif">
  <figure style="margin:0"><img src="scene.jpg" alt="" width="480" height="320"
    style="width:150px;height:150px;object-fit:fill;border:1px solid #999"><figcaption>fill (distorts)</figcaption></figure>
  <figure style="margin:0"><img src="scene.jpg" alt="" width="480" height="320"
    style="width:150px;height:150px;object-fit:contain;border:1px solid #999"><figcaption>contain</figcaption></figure>
  <figure style="margin:0"><img src="scene.jpg" alt="" width="480" height="320"
    style="width:150px;height:150px;object-fit:cover;object-position:80% 30%;border:1px solid #999"><figcaption>cover + position</figcaption></figure>
</div>
Rendered in your browser

When CSS forces an image into a box of a different shape, the object-fit property decides what happens: fill stretches it, contain letterboxes it and cover crops it, with object-position choosing which part to keep.65 The alt="" in this demo is deliberate, because the three images only illustrate the captions.

2.9 Lazy loading

The loading attribute has two states. eager, the default, fetches the image straight away; lazy lets the browser wait until the image is likely to be needed, typically as it comes close to the viewport.26,66 The standard only allows lazy loading when scripting is enabled, because otherwise a site could track how far a user had scrolled through the image requests it saw, a privacy leak that a script could already cause anyway.26 The same attribute works on iframe.16,26

Lazy, prioritised and asynchronously decoded imagesHTML
<!-- The hero image is the largest element in the first view: load it early -->
<img src="hero.avif" alt="…" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high">

<!-- Images further down the page: let the browser defer them -->
<img src="gallery-1.avif" alt="…" width="800" height="600" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
<img src="gallery-2.avif" alt="…" width="800" height="600" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
Do not lazy-load the heroThe largest image in the first screenful is often the page's Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) element. Marking it loading="lazy" delays it until layout is complete; web.dev recommends loading it eagerly, and raising its priority with fetchpriority="high".67–69

The decoding attribute is a hint about how the image should be decoded before it is shown: sync decodes it together with other page content, async allows other content to be shown first, and auto, the default, leaves the choice to the browser.70 fetchpriority tells the browser how important the request is relative to others of the same type: high, low or auto.27

2.10 Image optimisation

Images are usually the largest part of a page's download, so they repay attention.61 A practical checklist, drawing on MDN and web.dev:36,61,67,68

  1. Pick the right kind of format. Vector (SVG) for icons, logos and diagrams; a raster format for photographs.
  2. Use a modern codec with a fallback. AVIF or WebP, offered through picture with type, falling back to JPEG or PNG.
  3. Do not send more pixels than the screen can show. Generate several widths and offer them with srcset and an accurate sizes.
  4. Compress. For lossy formats, choose the lowest quality setting that still looks right; strip metadata such as EXIF data unless it is needed.
  5. Reserve the space. Always give width and height.
  6. Load in the right order. fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image; loading="lazy" on images below the fold.
  7. Cache. Serve images with long cache lifetimes and change the file name when the image changes.

2.11 Accessibility considerations

The W3C's Images Tutorial sorts images into seven types, each with its own approach to text alternatives.52

TypeApproachExample
Informative52A short description of the essential informationalt="Dog chasing a ball on a beach"
Decorative54Empty alt, or a CSS backgroundalt=""
Functional56The action or destination, not the picturealt="Print this page"
Images of text45,71The same text; better still, use real text styled with CSSalt="Summer sale: 20% off"
Complex55Short alt plus a long description in the pageChart with a data table below it
Groups of images50,52One alt for the group; empty alt for the restFive star icons: alt="4 out of 5 stars" on the first
Image maps52Alt on the img for the whole, and on each areaA floor plan with clickable rooms
A complex image: short alt, caption and a long descriptionHTML
<figure>
  <img src="scene.jpg" alt="Bar chart of file sizes by format; values in the table below"
       width="480" height="320" style="max-width:240px;height:auto">
  <figcaption>File size of one scene in five raster formats.</figcaption>
</figure>
<table>
  <caption>File sizes (kB)</caption>
  <tr><th>PNG</th><th>GIF</th><th>JPEG</th><th>WebP</th><th>AVIF</th></tr>
  <tr><td>121.3</td><td>72.2</td><td>10.8</td><td>6.2</td><td>4.3</td></tr>
</table>
Rendered in your browser
File sizes (kB)
PNGGIFJPEGWebPAVIF
121.372.210.86.24.3

(The image here stands in for a real chart.) A figure with a figcaption groups an image with its caption, and the caption gives the figure its accessible name; the image inside still needs its own alt.72,73 Other points worth remembering:29,38,51,52

  • Inline SVG used as an image needs role="img" and a name, from aria-label or a title element (the figures in this article use title and desc with aria-labelledby).
  • CSS background images cannot have alternative text, so only use them for decoration.
  • Do not put important information only in an image that may fail to load; the alt text is what users see when it does.
  • Animated images that move for more than five seconds need a way to pause them (WCAG 2.2.2), and nothing may flash more than three times a second (WCAG 2.3.1).46,47

3Audio and video

3.1 Media embedding: audio and video

FlowPhrasingEmbeddedInteractive (with controls)Content: source*, track*, fallback

A video element is used for playing videos or movies, and audio files with captions; an audio element represents a sound or audio stream.19,20 Both are media elements and share one API, HTMLMediaElement, with methods such as play() and pause() and properties such as currentTime, duration, volume and muted.22,74 The resource can be given by a src attribute or by child source elements, but not both; after the sources come zero or more track elements, then fallback content for browsers that do not support the element. Fallback content is not an accessibility feature: browsers that support media never show it.19,75

Table 7. Attributes of audio and video
AttributeOnValueEffect
srcbothURLThe media resource (or use source children)
controlsbothBooleanShow the browser's own playback controls
autoplaybothBooleanStart playing when possible, subject to the browser's autoplay policy
mutedbothBooleanStart with the sound muted (the default muted state)
loopbothBooleanSeek back to the start on reaching the end
preloadbothnone | metadata | autoHint: how much to download before playback
crossoriginbothanonymous | use-credentialsFetch with CORS (needed for cross-origin tracks and canvas use)
postervideoURLImage shown until the first frame is available
playsinlinevideoBooleanPlay in the page rather than going full screen (matters on iPhone)
width, heightvideoIntegersDimensions of the video's box, in CSS pixels

Source: HTML §4.8.8, §4.8.9 and §4.8.11.19,20,22

An audio player with two formatsHTML
<audio controls preload="metadata">
  <source src="tone.ogg" type="audio/ogg; codecs=opus">
  <source src="tone.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  <p>Your browser cannot play this audio.
     <a href="tone.mp3">Download the tone (MP3, 18 kB)</a>.</p>
</audio>
Rendered in your browser

This is a three-second C note (523 Hz), encoded twice for this article: as Opus in an Ogg container and as MP3. An audio element without controls is not displayed at all, so a sound effect played from a script needs no extra CSS.20,76

A video with sources, a poster, captions and subtitlesHTML
<video controls width="320" height="180" preload="metadata"
       poster="poster.jpg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto">
  <source src="clip.webm" type='video/webm; codecs="vp9, opus"'>
  <source src="clip.mp4" type='video/mp4; codecs="avc1.42E01E, mp4a.40.2"'>
  <track kind="captions" src="captions.en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English (CC)" default>
  <track kind="subtitles" src="subtitles.fr.vtt" srclang="fr" label="Français">
  <track kind="chapters" src="chapters.vtt" srclang="en" label="Chapters">
  <p>Your browser cannot play this video. <a href="clip.mp4">Download it (MP4, 80 kB)</a>.</p>
</video>
Rendered in your browser

The six-second test card has a 440 Hz tone, English captions turned on by default and French subtitles available from the player's captions menu. Every file it uses (two video encodings, a poster and three WebVTT files) is embedded in this page.

3.2 Media sources and formats

A media file is a container (such as MP4, WebM or Ogg) that holds one or more streams, each compressed with a codec (such as H.264, VP9 or AV1 for video, and AAC, Opus or MP3 for audio).77–79 The type attribute on source gives the container's MIME type and, optionally, a codecs parameter. The browser skips any source whose type it knows it cannot play, without downloading it; if the type is omitted, it has to fetch the file to find out.13,80,81

Table 8. Common web media formats
ContainerMIME typeTypical codecsNotes
MP4 (MPEG-4 Part 14)77video/mp4, audio/mp4H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, AV1; AACMost compatible; H.264 + AAC plays nearly everywhere
WebM77video/webm, audio/webmVP8, VP9, AV1; Opus, VorbisRoyalty-free; based on Matroska
Ogg77audio/ogg, video/oggOpus, Vorbis; TheoraMostly used for audio today
MP379audio/mpegMPEG-1 Audio Layer IIIUniversal support for audio
WAVE, FLAC77audio/wav, audio/flacPCM; FLACUncompressed and lossless audio; large files

Opus, standardised by the IETF in RFC 6716, is a royalty-free audio codec designed for both speech and music.82 Scripts can ask the browser whether it can play a type with canPlayType(), which returns "probably", "maybe" or the empty string; the cautious answers reflect the fact that a browser cannot be sure until it tries the actual file.80,83 This table asks your browser:

Table 9. canPlayType() results in your browser (filled in by script)
Type stringResult
video/mp4; codecs="avc1.42E01E, mp4a.40.2"…
video/webm; codecs="vp9, opus"…
video/mp4; codecs="av01.0.05M.08"…
video/mp4; codecs="hvc1.1.6.L93.B0"…
audio/ogg; codecs=opus…
audio/mpeg…
audio/flac…
video/x-flv…
Order your sourcesPut the most efficient format first (for example AV1 or VP9 in WebM) and the most compatible last (H.264 in MP4). Browsers take the first source they can play, so the reverse order would mean every browser chose the larger file.81,84

3.3 Playback controls

The boolean controls attribute asks the browser to provide its own user interface: play and pause, seeking, volume, captions, full screen and, in some browsers, picture-in-picture. The standard expects these controls to be keyboard-accessible and exposed to assistive technology.85 Without controls, a video shows no interface, though browsers may still offer controls through a context menu.85 Sites that build their own controls must make them operable by keyboard and give each one an accessible name and state.86–88

Custom controls built on the media APIHTML
<div class="custom-player">
  <video id="cp-video" width="320" height="180" preload="metadata" playsinline
         poster="poster.jpg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;display:block">
    <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">
    <source src="clip.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
  </video>
  <div class="cp-bar">
    <button type="button" id="cp-play">Play</button>
    <button type="button" id="cp-mute" aria-pressed="false">Mute</button>
    <button type="button" id="cp-cc" aria-pressed="false">Captions</button>
    <label>Seek <input id="cp-seek" type="range" min="0" max="6" step="0.1" value="0"></label>
    <output id="cp-time">0.0 / 6.0 s</output>
  </div>
</div>
Rendered in your browser
0.0 / 6.0 s
The script behind the custom controlsJS
const v = document.getElementById("cp-video");
playBtn.onclick = () => v.paused ? v.play() : v.pause();
v.onplay  = () => playBtn.textContent = "Pause";
v.onpause = () => playBtn.textContent = "Play";
muteBtn.onclick = () => { v.muted = !v.muted; muteBtn.setAttribute("aria-pressed", v.muted); };
ccBtn.onclick = () => {
  const t = v.textTracks[0];
  t.mode = t.mode === "showing" ? "hidden" : "showing";
  ccBtn.setAttribute("aria-pressed", t.mode === "showing");
};
seek.oninput = () => v.currentTime = seek.valueAsNumber;
v.ontimeupdate = () => { seek.value = v.currentTime; out.value = v.currentTime.toFixed(1) + " / " + v.duration.toFixed(1) + " s"; };

Real buttons give keyboard access and a role for free; aria-pressed exposes the on/off state of the toggles; and the play button's label changes with the state. A text track's mode can be "showing", "hidden" (loaded, cues fire events, nothing drawn) or "disabled".74,89

3.4 Autoplay

The autoplay attribute asks the browser to start playback as soon as it can without stopping.90 The standard lets browsers give users a way to override or disable autoplay,90,91 and every major browser now has an autoplay policy. Chrome's, for example, always allows muted autoplay, and allows autoplay with sound only if the user has interacted with the site (a click or tap), has a high enough Media Engagement Index from previously playing media with sound there, or has installed the site.92 MDN summarises the common rule across browsers: media may autoplay if its audio is muted or its volume is zero, if the user has interacted with the site, or if the site is allowed by the user or by a permissions policy.93

Detecting a blocked autoplayJS
const video = document.querySelector("video");
video.play().catch(err => {
  if (err.name === "NotAllowedError") {
    // Autoplay with sound was blocked: show a play button,
    // or retry muted.
    video.muted = true;
    return video.play();
  }
});

play() returns a promise, which is rejected with a NotAllowedError when the browser's policy blocks playback, so a page can fall back gracefully.90,93 For embedded players, the autoplay feature of Permissions Policy controls whether a cross-origin iframe may autoplay; the embedding page grants it with allow="autoplay".93,95

Autoplay and accessibilitySound that starts by itself makes it hard for screen-reader users to hear their screen reader. If audio plays automatically for more than three seconds, WCAG 1.4.2 requires a way to pause or stop it, or to control its volume separately from the system volume.44 Moving video that starts automatically and lasts more than five seconds needs a pause control too (WCAG 2.2.2).46

3.5 Muted playback

The muted content attribute sets the media element's default muted state when it is created; it does not track later changes. The muted property in script reflects whether the element is currently muted, and the defaultMuted property reflects the attribute.22,74 So a script that unmutes a video changes video.muted but leaves the attribute in the markup. Muting is what makes autoplay reliable: WebKit's 2016 change to iOS policy allowed <video muted autoplay> and videos without audio tracks to start without a user gesture, and introduced playsinline so iPhone users would not be thrown into full screen.94

3.6 Looping

With the loop attribute, a media element seeks back to the start of the resource when it reaches the end, instead of stopping.90 Combined with autoplay, muted and playsinline, it gives a silent, looping clip that behaves like an animated GIF at a fraction of the size.61,93

A GIF replacement: silent, looping, inline, with a pause buttonHTML
<video id="gif-like" autoplay muted loop playsinline width="320" height="180"
       aria-label="Animated test card" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;display:block">
  <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="clip.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
<button type="button" onclick="var v=document.getElementById('gif-like');
  v.paused ? v.play() : v.pause(); this.textContent = v.paused ? 'Play animation' : 'Pause animation'">Pause animation</button>
Rendered in your browser

The button keeps the loop within WCAG 2.2.2, because the animation starts automatically and runs for more than five seconds.46 Users who have asked their operating system to reduce motion can be respected too, with the prefers-reduced-motion media query in CSS or script.

3.7 Video poster images

The poster attribute gives the URL of an image that the browser shows while no video data is available, typically before the user presses play. The standard describes it as a representative frame of the video.19 Without a poster, a video that has loaded its first frame shows that frame instead; with preload="none" and no poster, users see an empty box.19,84 A poster is a good partner for preload="none" on pages that hold many videos: nothing but the image is downloaded until the user chooses to play.84

Table 10. The preload hint
ValueMeaningUse when
noneThe author expects the user not to play it, or wants to minimise trafficMany videos on one page
metadataFetch dimensions, duration and the first frame onlyThe usual default
auto (or empty)The browser may download the whole resourceThe video is the page's main content

Source: HTML §4.8.11.5. The value is only a hint, and autoplay overrides it.81

3.8 The track element

Void (no end tag)Only inside audio or video, after any source

The track element lets authors specify explicit external timed text tracks for media elements.21 Its attributes are kind, src (required), srclang, label and default. The track file is fetched in CORS mode, so a track from another origin works only if the server sends the right CORS headers and the media element has a crossorigin attribute.21,96

Table 11. Values of the kind attribute
kindForShown by the browser?
subtitles (default)Translation of the dialogue, for viewers who can hear but do not understand the languageYes, when selected
captionsDialogue, sound effects, music and speaker identification, for viewers who cannot hearYes, when selected
descriptionsText descriptions of the video, intended to be read out (for example by a screen reader)Not drawn on the video
chaptersChapter titles, for navigating the mediaIn a chapter menu, where supported
metadataData for scriptsNo

Source: HTML §4.8.10. srclang is required for subtitles. If kind is missing the track is subtitles; if it has an unknown value, it is metadata.21

3.9 Captions and subtitles: WebVTT

The format for track files is WebVTT, the Web Video Text Tracks Format, served with the MIME type text/vtt.30,97 A WebVTT file starts with the line WEBVTT, then a blank line, then cues separated by blank lines. Each cue has an optional identifier, a timing line (start --> end, with optional settings) and one or more lines of text.30,97

captions.en.vtt (used by the video in section 3.1)VTT
WEBVTT

00:00.000 --> 00:02.000
[Steady 440 Hz tone]
This is the test card.

00:02.000 --> 00:04.000 line:10%
Captions describe speech
<i>and</i> important sounds.

00:04.000 --> 00:06.000
The tone ends. [Silence]
Styling cues with ::cueCSS
video::cue {
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.8);
  color: #fff;
  font: 1.1em/1.3 system-ui, sans-serif;
}
video::cue(i) { color: #fde68a; }

The ::cue pseudo-element styles cue text, with a limited set of properties (colour, background, font, text decoration and a few others).30,97 Keep cue styling modest: captions must stay readable over any frame of the video.

3.10 Web accessibility and captions

The W3C's guide to accessible media lists what each audience needs.98 People who are deaf or hard of hearing need captions for video and transcripts for audio. People who are blind or have low vision need audio description of important visual information that the soundtrack does not convey. People who are deafblind need a transcript that includes both the dialogue and the visual information, because it can be read on a braille display. Everyone needs an accessible media player that works with a keyboard and a screen reader.48,88,98–100

Table 12. What WCAG 2.2 requires for prerecorded media
MediaLevel ALevel AA
Audio only (podcast)Transcript (1.2.1)—
Video only (silent animation)Transcript or audio track (1.2.1)—
Video with audioCaptions (1.2.2); audio description or full text alternative (1.2.3)Audio description (1.2.5)
Live video with audio—Captions (1.2.4)

Sources: WCAG 2.2 Understanding documents for 1.2.1 to 1.2.5.39–43

Avoid

Inaccessible mediaHTML
<video src="talk.mp4" autoplay>
  Sorry, no captions.
</video>

No controls, sound that starts by itself, no captions, and fallback text that users of modern browsers never see.40,44,75

Prefer

Accessible mediaHTML
<figure>
  <video controls preload="metadata" poster="talk.jpg">
    <source src="talk.webm" type="video/webm">
    <source src="talk.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="talk.en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
    <track kind="descriptions" src="talk.desc.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio description">
  </video>
  <figcaption>Keynote (12 min). <a href="talk-transcript.html">Read the transcript</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

Controls, captions on by default, descriptions, and a transcript link next to the video that everyone can see.48,99,100

Automatic captions are a draftSpeech recognition produces captions quickly, but the W3C guidance is that automatic captions alone are not sufficient: they need human review and correction before they meet user needs and WCAG.48

4Embedded content

4.1 The iframe element

FlowPhrasingEmbeddedInteractiveContent: nothing

The iframe element represents its content navigable: a nested browsing context holding a complete document of its own.16 The document comes from the URL in src, or from the HTML written directly into srcdoc, which wins if both are present. Its other attributes are name, sandbox, allow, allowfullscreen, width, height, referrerpolicy and loading.16 An iframe has no fallback content: anything between its tags is ignored.16,101

An iframe with srcdoc and a titleHTML
<iframe title="A tiny embedded document" width="320" height="90" style="border:1px solid #999;max-width:100%"
        srcdoc="<p style='font:15px system-ui;margin:10px'>Hello from a <b>nested document</b>.</p>"></iframe>
Rendered in your browser

Every iframe needs a title that describes its content, because screen readers announce it when the user moves into the frame (WCAG technique H64).87,102 The default size, if no width or height is set, is 300 × 150 CSS pixels.101

The sandbox attribute

When sandbox is present, the framed content is placed under extra restrictions. An empty sandbox applies all of them: the content gets a unique opaque origin (so it cannot read cookies or storage for its real origin), scripts do not run, forms cannot be submitted, popups cannot open, and the content cannot navigate the top-level page. Each keyword in the attribute lifts one restriction.16 The standard defines thirteen keywords:

Table 13. sandbox keywords
KeywordAllows
allow-scriptsRunning scripts
allow-same-originTreating the content as its real origin instead of an opaque one
allow-formsSubmitting forms
allow-popups, allow-popups-to-escape-sandboxOpening new windows; letting them be unsandboxed
allow-modalsalert(), confirm(), print() and similar dialogs
allow-top-navigation, allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation, allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocolsNavigating the top-level page (always, only after a user gesture, or to non-HTTP schemes)
allow-downloadsStarting downloads
allow-orientation-lock, allow-pointer-lock, allow-presentationLocking screen orientation, the Pointer Lock API, presentation sessions

Source: HTML §4.8.5 The iframe element.16

The same document, sandboxed and notHTML
<iframe title="Sandboxed: scripts blocked" sandbox="" width="230" height="60" style="border:1px solid #999"
        srcdoc="<p id='o' style='font:14px system-ui'>Scripts are blocked.</p><script>document.getElementById('o').textContent='Scripts ran.'</script>"></iframe>
<iframe title="Sandboxed with allow-scripts" sandbox="allow-scripts" width="230" height="60" style="border:1px solid #999"
        srcdoc="<p id='o' style='font:14px system-ui'>Scripts are blocked.</p><script>document.getElementById('o').textContent='Scripts ran: origin is '+location.origin</script>"></iframe>
Rendered in your browser

The second frame runs its script but reports its origin as null, the opaque origin that sandboxing gives it.16,103

Never combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin for same-origin contentIf the framed page has the same origin as its parent, these two keywords together let its scripts reach up and remove the sandbox attribute, which makes the sandbox useless. The standard warns against exactly this combination.16

The allow attribute

The allow attribute sets a Permissions Policy for the frame, delegating powerful features such as the camera, geolocation, full screen or autoplay to the embedded page. By default, most such features are not available to cross-origin frames.16,95 The older allowfullscreen attribute is equivalent to allow="fullscreen *".16

Delegating features to an embedded video playerHTML
<iframe src="https://player.example/embed/abc123"
        title="Product demo video (2 minutes)"
        width="560" height="315"
        allow="autoplay; fullscreen; picture-in-picture; encrypted-media"
        referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
        loading="lazy"></iframe>

4.2 The embed element

FlowPhrasingEmbeddedInteractiveVoid (no end tag)

The embed element provides an integration point for an external application or interactive content, historically a plugin.17 It is a void element with just four attributes of its own: src, type, width and height. It has no fallback content and no way to give a text alternative except through ARIA.17,104 Browsers have removed support for plugins such as Flash, so today embed mainly displays content the browser can handle itself, such as images, SVG documents and, in browsers with a built-in viewer, PDFs.33,104

embed showing an SVG documentHTML
<embed src="scene.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="240" height="160">
Rendered in your browser

4.3 The object element

FlowPhrasingEmbeddedListed (form)Content: transparent fallback

The object element can represent an external resource, which, depending on the type of the resource, is treated as an image or as a child navigable (a nested document).18 Its main attributes are data (the URL), type, name, form, width and height. Unlike embed, its content is fallback content: if the resource cannot be shown, the browser renders the element's children instead.18,32

object with fallback contentHTML
<object data="scene.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="240" height="160">
  <img src="scene.jpg" alt="Green hills under a yellow sun" width="240" height="160">
</object>
<object data="missing-file.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="240" height="60">
  <p>No PDF viewer here. <a href="missing-file.pdf">Download the PDF</a>.</p>
</object>
Rendered in your browser

The second object points at a file that does not exist, so its fallback paragraph appears. Fallback chains like this were how sites once offered Flash with a video or image inside it for devices without the plugin.32

4.4 The canvas element

FlowPhrasingEmbeddedContent: transparent fallback

The canvas element provides scripts with a resolution-dependent bitmap canvas, which can be used for rendering graphs, game graphics, art or other visual images on the fly.6 It has only two attributes, width and height, which set the size of the bitmap in pixels and default to 300 and 150. Drawing happens through a context obtained with getContext(): "2d", "webgl", "webgl2" or "bitmaprenderer" (WebGPU adds "webgpu").6,105 The standard tells authors not to use canvas when a more suitable element is available, such as rendering a page heading as text.6

A canvas chart with fallback contentHTML
<canvas id="bar-canvas" width="320" height="140" role="img"
        aria-label="Bar chart: PNG 121 kB, GIF 72 kB, JPEG 11 kB, WebP 6 kB, AVIF 4 kB">
  <table>
    <caption>File size (kB)</caption>
    <tr><th>PNG</th><td>121</td></tr><tr><th>GIF</th><td>72</td></tr>
    <tr><th>JPEG</th><td>11</td></tr><tr><th>WebP</th><td>6</td></tr><tr><th>AVIF</th><td>4</td></tr>
  </table>
</canvas>
<script>
(function () {
  var c = document.getElementById("bar-canvas"), g = c.getContext("2d");
  var data = [["PNG",121],["GIF",72],["JPEG",11],["WebP",6],["AVIF",4]];
  g.font = "12px system-ui, sans-serif";
  data.forEach(function (d, i) {
    var y = 10 + i * 26;
    g.fillStyle = "#6b7280"; g.fillText(d[0], 4, y + 13);
    g.fillStyle = ["#6b7280","#b7791f","#2457a6","#2f7d4f","#b4441f"][i];
    g.fillRect(48, y, d[1] * 2, 18);
    g.fillStyle = "#6b7280"; g.fillText(d[1] + " kB", 54 + d[1] * 2, y + 13);
  });
})();
</script>
Rendered in your browser
File size (kB)
PNG121
GIF72
JPEG11
WebP6
AVIF4

A canvas is a flat bitmap: assistive technology sees nothing of what is drawn. The content between the tags is exposed instead, and may contain focusable elements, so a chart can carry its data table as fallback; role="img" with an aria-label gives the whole canvas a short name.6,106 For anything interactive, real DOM elements or SVG are usually more accessible than a canvas.106

4.5 Inline svg

An svg element in an HTML document is parsed into the SVG namespace and becomes part of the page's DOM, as defined by the SVG 2 specification; HTML §4.8.16 describes how the two languages fit together.23,29 Because it is part of the page, inline SVG can be styled by the page's CSS (including currentColor, hover states and dark mode), animated and scripted, and its text can be selected and searched. That is the opposite of an SVG loaded through img, which is isolated and static.14,107

Inline SVG styled by the pageHTML
<style>
  .icon-demo { color: #2457a6; }
  .icon-demo:hover { color: #b4441f; }
  .icon-demo svg { width: 48px; height: 48px; vertical-align: middle; }
</style>
<p class="icon-demo">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" role="img" aria-labelledby="sun-title">
    <title id="sun-title">Sun</title>
    <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="5" fill="currentColor"/>
    <g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round">
      <line x1="12" y1="1" x2="12" y2="4"/><line x1="12" y1="20" x2="12" y2="23"/>
      <line x1="1" y1="12" x2="4" y2="12"/><line x1="20" y1="12" x2="23" y2="12"/>
    </g>
  </svg>
  Hover me: the icon follows the text colour.
</p>
Rendered in your browser

Hover me: the icon follows the text colour.

Table 14. Five ways to put SVG on a page
MethodScripts run?Page CSS applies?Cached separately?Text alternative
<img src="x.svg">NoNoYesalt
CSS background-imageNoNoYesNone (decoration only)
Inline <svg>Yes (page scripts)YesNorole="img" + title or aria-label
<object data="x.svg">Yes (its own)NoYesFallback content, ARIA
<iframe src="x.svg">Yes (its own)NoYestitle

Sources: MDN, SVG in HTML; HTML §4.8.3, §4.8.7 and §4.8.16.14,18,23,107

4.6 External content embedding

Video hosts, maps, social networks and payment providers offer "embed codes", which are almost always an iframe pointing at their own domain.108 Embedding third-party content brings three costs worth managing:

  1. Performance. Each embed loads a whole document with its own scripts. Give off-screen embeds loading="lazy", or show a lightweight placeholder (an image with a play button) and create the real iframe only when the user clicks it.26,67
  2. Privacy. The embedded site can set cookies and see that the user visited your page. Some providers offer a reduced-tracking mode; YouTube's privacy-enhanced mode, for example, uses the youtube-nocookie.com domain.109 referrerpolicy limits what the referrer header reveals.16
  3. Security. Grant only the features the embed needs with allow, and use sandbox when the content is not fully trusted.16,95
A privacy-conscious video embedHTML
<iframe width="560" height="315"
        src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
        title="How we built the Kettlemaster 3000 (video, 4 minutes)"
        allow="accelerometer; autoplay; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture"
        allowfullscreen
        referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
        loading="lazy"
        style="max-width:100%; height:auto; aspect-ratio:16/9"></iframe>

4.7 Cross-origin considerations

Two URLs have the same origin when their scheme, host and port all match.103,110 The same-origin policy lets a page embed resources from other origins (images, media, scripts, frames) but generally stops it reading them.111 The rules differ by element:

Table 15. Cross-origin controls for embedded content
ControlSet byEffect
crossorigin attribute25,115Embedding pageFetch img, audio, video or script in CORS mode (anonymous without cookies, use-credentials with)
Access-Control-Allow-Origin113,116Resource's serverAllows the named origin to read the response, so a canvas stays origin-clean
Tainted canvas112BrowsergetImageData(), toDataURL() and toBlob() throw a SecurityError after a non-CORS cross-origin image is drawn
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy117Resource's serverTells browsers not to let other sites (or origins) embed the resource at all
X-Frame-Options118,119Framed page's serverDENY or SAMEORIGIN: refuse to be shown in other sites' frames (protects against clickjacking)
CSP frame-ancestors120,121Framed page's serverThe modern, more flexible replacement for X-Frame-Options
postMessage()122Both pagesThe safe way for a page and a cross-origin frame to talk; always check event.origin
sandbox, allow, referrerpolicy16,95Embedding pageRestrict what a frame can do, which features it gets, and what referrer it sees
Reading pixels from a cross-origin imageJS
const img = new Image();
img.crossOrigin = "anonymous";           // same as crossorigin="anonymous"
img.src = "https://cdn.other.example/photo.jpg";
img.onload = () => {
  const c = document.createElement("canvas");
  c.width = img.naturalWidth; c.height = img.naturalHeight;
  const g = c.getContext("2d");
  g.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
  // Works only if the server answered with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  // Without crossOrigin, or without the header, this line throws SecurityError.
  const pixel = g.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1).data;
};

Media elements follow the same rule: a cross-origin video drawn onto a canvas taints it unless it was fetched with CORS, and cross-origin track files need CORS to load at all.21,112

5Putting it together: a product page

The page below combines the main techniques in this article: a responsive, format-switched hero image with dimensions and high fetch priority; a decorative image with empty alt; lazily loaded gallery images; a captioned video with a poster and a transcript link; a sound clip; an inline SVG icon; and a sandboxed third-party embed. It is rendered in a sandboxed frame.

A product page with images, video, audio and an embedHTML
<style>
  body { max-width: 640px; }
  img, video { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
  .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 6px; }
  .rating svg { width: 18px; height: 18px; fill: #b7791f; vertical-align: -3px; }
  figure { margin: 1em 0; } figcaption { font-size: .9em; color: #555; }
</style>
<header>
  <h1>Kettlemaster 3000</h1>
  <p class="rating">
    <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" role="img" aria-label="Rated 4 out of 5"><path d="M12 2l3 7h7l-5.5 4.5L18 21l-6-4-6 4 1.5-7.5L2 9h7z"/></svg>
    4.0 (212 reviews)
  </p>
</header>

<picture>
  <source srcset="scene.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="scene.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="scene.jpg" width="480" height="320" fetchpriority="high"
       alt="The Kettlemaster 3000 on a windowsill, hills and sunset behind it">
</picture>

<p><img src="scene.svg" alt="" width="60" height="40" style="vertical-align:middle">
   Boils a litre in 90 seconds.</p>

<h2>Gallery</h2>
<div class="gallery">
  <img src="scene.jpg" alt="Side view" width="480" height="320" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  <img src="scene-crop.jpg" alt="Close-up of the spout" width="280" height="280" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  <img src="scene.webp" alt="In a kitchen at dusk" width="480" height="320" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
</div>

<h2>See it in action</h2>
<figure>
  <video controls preload="none" width="320" height="180" poster="poster.jpg">
    <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">
    <source src="clip.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  </video>
  <figcaption>Demo (6 seconds). <a href="#transcript">Read the transcript</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>Hear the whistle</h2>
<audio controls preload="none">
  <source src="tone.ogg" type="audio/ogg; codecs=opus">
  <source src="tone.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
</audio>
<p>A three-second whistle in C.</p>

<h2>Find a stockist</h2>
<iframe title="Stockist map (third-party content)" width="320" height="80" sandbox loading="lazy"
        srcdoc="<p style='font:14px system-ui;margin:8px'>Third-party map would load here.</p>"
        style="border:1px solid #ccc"></iframe>

<h2 id="transcript">Transcript</h2>
<p>[A steady 440 Hz tone plays over a colour test card.] This is the test card.
   Captions describe speech and important sounds. [The tone ends.]</p>
Rendered in a sandboxed frame

Count the decisions: one image is prioritised, three are deferred, one is silenced with alt=""; the video downloads nothing but its poster until it is played; and the transcript serves deafblind users and anyone who prefers reading.26,54,68,81,99 The star icon's aria-label carries the rating, because a colour alone would mean nothing to a screen reader.52

6Exercises

Try each exercise before opening its solution. You can test markup in the playground and image selection in the srcset simulator.

Exercise 1: Write the alt text

Write a suitable alt for each image.

  1. A magnifying-glass icon that is the only content of a search button.
  2. A photo of the CEO next to the caption "Ana Ruiz, CEO", which is in a figcaption.
  3. A swirly divider between two sections.
  4. The company logo, linking to the home page.
  5. A line chart of monthly visitors with the full data in a table just below it.
Show solution
Solution 1HTML
<button><img src="search.svg" alt="Search"></button>
<figure><img src="ana.jpg" alt="Ana Ruiz smiling at her desk"><figcaption>Ana Ruiz, CEO</figcaption></figure>
<img src="divider.svg" alt="">
<a href="/"><img src="logo.svg" alt="Example Co. home"></a>
<img src="visitors.png" alt="Line chart: monthly visitors doubled in 2026; data in the table below">

(a) A functional image describes the action.56 (b) The caption already names her, so alt can describe what the photo adds, or be empty if it adds nothing.50 (c) Decoration is silenced.54 (d) A logo link names the destination.56 (e) A complex image gets a short alt that points to the long description.55

Exercise 2: Fix the responsive image

This image shows at 100% width on phones and at a fixed 400px column on screens 900px wide and up. What is wrong, and what should sizes be?

Exercise 2HTML
<img src="dog-800.jpg"
     srcset="dog-400.jpg 400w, dog-800.jpg 800w, dog-1600.jpg 2x"
     alt="A dog asleep in the sun">
Show solution

Three problems: the list mixes w and x descriptors, which is not allowed; sizes is missing, so the browser assumes 100vw and downloads a far larger file than the 400px column needs on desktop; and width/height are missing, so the page shifts when it loads.57,63

Solution 2HTML
<img src="dog-800.jpg"
     srcset="dog-400.jpg 400w, dog-800.jpg 800w, dog-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(min-width: 900px) 400px, 100vw"
     width="1600" height="1067"
     alt="A dog asleep in the sun">

Exercise 3: Which candidate?

With srcset="s.jpg 480w, m.jpg 960w, l.jpg 1920w" and sizes="(min-width: 800px) 50vw, 100vw", which file is the ideal choice for (a) a 375px-wide phone at DPR 3; (b) a 1280px-wide laptop at DPR 1; (c) a 1280px-wide laptop at DPR 2?

Show solution

(a) 375px viewport: the condition fails, so the slot is 100vw = 375px; densities are 1.28x, 2.56x, 5.12x; the smallest at least 3x is l.jpg. (b) Slot = 50vw = 640px; densities 0.75x, 1.5x, 3x; the smallest at least 1x is m.jpg. (c) Same slot, need 2x: l.jpg (3x). A browser may still pick a smaller file to save data.58 Check your answers in the simulator.

Exercise 4: Format switching

Write a picture that offers hero.avif, then hero.webp, with hero.jpg as the fallback. The image is 1200 × 600, is the page's main image and has the alt text "Mountain lake at dawn".

Show solution
Solution 4HTML
<picture>
  <source srcset="hero.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="hero.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="hero.jpg" width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high"
       alt="Mountain lake at dawn">
</picture>

The alt, dimensions and priority go on the img, which is the element that is rendered. The main image is not lazy-loaded.12,68

Exercise 5: Replace the GIF

A 4 MB animated GIF, demo.gif, shows a looping screen recording with no sound. Replace it with video that autoplays reliably on all browsers, including iPhone, and meets WCAG 2.2.2.

Show solution
Solution 5HTML
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline width="800" height="450"
       aria-label="Screen recording: dragging a file onto the upload area">
  <source src="demo.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
<button type="button" id="pause-demo">Pause animation</button>

muted makes autoplay allowed; playsinline stops iPhone going full screen; a pause control is needed because the loop runs for more than five seconds. (Adding controls would also satisfy 2.2.2.)46,93,94

Exercise 6: Make the video accessible

Improve this markup for a 10-minute lecture with speech. List what you added and which WCAG criterion each addresses.

Exercise 6HTML
<video src="lecture.mp4" autoplay></video>
Show solution
Solution 6HTML
<video controls preload="metadata" poster="lecture.jpg">
  <source src="lecture.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="lecture.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="lecture.en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  <track kind="descriptions" src="lecture.desc.vtt" srclang="en" label="Descriptions">
</video>
<p><a href="lecture-transcript.html">Transcript</a></p>

Removed autoplay (1.4.2 Audio Control); added controls (2.1.1 Keyboard, 2.2.2); captions (1.2.2); a description track or audio-described version plus a transcript (1.2.3, 1.2.5). Note that WCAG 1.2.5 expects audio description in the audio itself; a text description track helps only where the player reads it out.40,41,43,44,86,100

Exercise 7: Write a WebVTT file

Write captions for a 5-second clip: from 0 to 2.5 seconds a speaker called Sam says "Welcome back"; from 2.5 to 5 seconds a door slams.

Show solution
Solution 7VTT
WEBVTT

00:00.000 --> 00:02.500
<v Sam>Welcome back.

00:02.500 --> 00:05.000
[Door slams]

The file must start with WEBVTT; the voice tag identifies the speaker, and the sound effect goes in brackets because captions are for viewers who cannot hear it.30,48

Exercise 8: Sandbox an untrusted widget

You must embed a third-party poll from https://poll.example/w/42. It needs to run scripts and submit a form, and may open its results in a new tab. It must not navigate your page, use the camera or know which page it was embedded on. Write the iframe.

Show solution
Solution 8HTML
<iframe src="https://poll.example/w/42" title="Reader poll: favourite kettle colour"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms allow-popups allow-same-origin"
        referrerpolicy="no-referrer" loading="lazy" width="400" height="300"></iframe>

allow-same-origin is safe here because the poll's origin differs from yours; it lets the poll use its own cookies. Leaving out the allow-top-navigation keywords blocks navigation of your page; giving no allow attribute leaves the camera disabled for the cross-origin frame; no-referrer hides your page's URL.16,95

Exercise 9: Why does toDataURL fail?

A script draws https://images.other.example/a.jpg onto a canvas and calls canvas.toDataURL(), which throws a SecurityError. What two changes fix it?

Show solution

The page must request the image with CORS, by setting crossorigin="anonymous" (or img.crossOrigin = "anonymous") before setting src; and the image server must respond with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that allows the page's origin. Without both, the canvas is tainted.25,112,114

Exercise 10: Choose the element

Which element fits each case best: img, picture, video, iframe, object, canvas or inline svg?

  1. An icon that must change colour with the surrounding text.
  2. A photo that needs a square crop on phones.
  3. A real-time particle animation in a game.
  4. A map from a mapping service.
  5. A PDF preview with a download link as fallback.
Show solution

(a) Inline svg with currentColor.107 (b) picture with a media source (art direction).12 (c) canvas.6 (d) iframe, the provider's embed.16 (e) object, whose children are fallback content.18

7Trivia questions

  1. Who proposed the IMG tag, and when?

    Answer

    Marc Andreessen, in a message to the www-talk mailing list on 25 February 1993.2

  2. Which of these elements has no end tag: img, video, source, track, embed, iframe?

    Answer

    img, source, track and embed are void elements. video and iframe need end tags.13,14,17,21

  3. What is the default size of a canvas bitmap?

    Answer

    300 × 150 pixels.6

  4. How many keywords does the sandbox attribute define?

    Answer

    Thirteen, from allow-downloads to allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocols.16

  5. What does sizes default to when it is missing?

    Answer

    100vw, the full viewport width.57

  6. Which company introduced the GIF format, and in what year?

    Answer

    CompuServe, in 1987 (GIF87a); the 89a revision added animation-related extensions and transparency.28,37

  7. What MIME type does a WebVTT file use, and what must its first line be?

    Answer

    text/vtt; the first line is WEBVTT.30,97

  8. What is the kind of a track element with no kind attribute? With kind="banana"?

    Answer

    subtitles, and metadata.21

  9. Which three strings can canPlayType() return?

    Answer

    "probably", "maybe" and the empty string.83

  10. Why does the standard only allow lazy-loading of images when scripting is enabled?

    Answer

    To avoid creating a new way to track a user's scroll position through image requests in a browser where scripts are turned off.26

  11. What origin does a document in <iframe sandbox> report?

    Answer

    null: an opaque origin, unless allow-same-origin is given.16,103

  12. Which IETF RFC defines the WebP format, and when was it published?

    Answer

    RFC 9649, in November 2024.9

  13. On which date did Adobe stop supporting Flash Player?

    Answer

    31 December 2020.33

  14. Which HTTP header lets a page refuse to be shown in other sites' frames, and what replaced it?

    Answer

    X-Frame-Options (RFC 7034), largely replaced by the CSP frame-ancestors directive.118,120,121

  15. The muted attribute is removed by a script after the page loads. Does the video unmute?

    Answer

    No. The attribute only sets the default muted state; the current state is the muted property.22,74

  16. What does WCAG's first success criterion require?

    Answer

    1.1.1 Non-text Content: a text alternative that serves the same purpose for all non-text content, with some exceptions such as decoration.38

8srcset simulator

Enter a srcset with width descriptors and a sizes value, then pick a viewport width and device-pixel ratio. The simulator evaluates sizes with your browser's own media-query engine at the chosen width, converts each candidate to a density and shows the candidate a browser would ideally choose: the smallest one whose density is at least the device-pixel ratio, or the largest if none is.57,58 Real browsers may choose differently, for example to save data.

375 px
Presets:

9Playground

Type HTML on the left. The right pane shows the rendered result in a sandboxed frame, and the bottom pane shows the DOM tree your browser's parser built.123 The presets use real images and media embedded in this page.

Updates as you type

In the presets, short names such as scene.jpg are replaced with the embedded files before rendering, and are shown as data: URLs in the DOM tree.

Sources: HTML Living Standard §2.5, §4.8 and §4.12.5; W3C WebVTT; WCAG 2.2.3,6,11,16,21,22,30,57

Responsive images in one breath

Several widths in srcset, an honest sizes, width and height on the img, modern formats through picture.12,24,57

Good alt text

Describes the purpose in context, is short, does not start with "image of", and is empty for decoration. Complex images get a long description in the page.50,52,55

Media checklist

controls; no unmuted autoplay; captions on by default; audio description; a visible transcript link; a pause button for looping clips.40,44,46,98

Performance

Prioritise the hero, lazy-load the rest, replace GIFs with video, use preload="none" plus a poster for many videos.67,68,81

Third-party embeds

Title every frame; grant only the features needed with allow; sandbox when in doubt; lazy-load; prefer privacy-enhanced modes.16,95,102,109
